newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's MRTA has 70 crisis back-up fighters in Lima.
newsitem.headline: Peru's MRTA has 70 crisis back-up fighters in Lima.

text.p: A Marxist rebel group holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home has moved at least 70 fighters into the Peruvian capital to back up comrades inside the residence, a secret intelligence report said.

The two-page National Intelligence Service report dated March 12 and obtained by Reuters on Friday said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) transported "by different means personnel and arms to form 'External Support Groups.'"

The groups would act as back-up for about 20 rebels holed up inside the residence for 101 days in case talks to peacefully end Latin America's longest hostage siege "do not reach a good conclusion," the report said.

The MRTA stormed the mansion Dec. 17 and took hundreds of party guests hostage to demand the release of 450 jailed comrades, it said. Most of the hostages were released in the early weeks of the siege.
Rebels planned the operation for close to a year and, according to the intelligence report, 70 fighters meant to act as external support arrived in Lima in three groups starting last October.
An earlier intelligence report, dated Feb. 21 and obtained by Reuters earlier this month, put the number at 50 fighters.
A squad of "nine or 10" Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels travelled to Lima between October and November 1996 from northern Peru, the report said.

Another group of about 50 fighters, led by a woman rebel with the nom de guerre "La Gringa," reached the capital in February from an MRTA stronghold on the west bank of the Perene River in Peru's central jungle, it said. This unit's presence in Lima was revealed in the prior report.

A third group of 10 rebels, also from the central jungle districts of Chanchamayo and San Ramon, arrived March 2 in a pick-up truck and were dropped off in a slum in eastern Lima, the latest report said.
It added that 12 rifles were brought by truck to Lima's outskirts in February, transferred to a car and taken to the same slum. The earlier report also referred to a shipment of a dozen rifles.

The fighters would "carry out significant terrorist acts to raise the awareness of public opinion so it supports the demands of the group led by (rebel leader) Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in the discussions now underway," it said.
The support groups may seize radio and television stations to "disseminate proclamations and messages," it added.
Face-to-face talks between the government and MRTA stalled March 12 when the rebels accused Peru's security forces of digging a tunnel to storm the residence and free the hostages.
Direct negotiations are expected to resume early next week and optimism has sprouted in Lima diplomatic and media circles that a deal to end the crisis may be in the offing.

Rebels and President Alberto Fujimori both said the two sides were moving closer but problems remained and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he did not foresee dramatic progress soon in the upcoming talks.
